108274.e: Reflux comes from the Latin word for flowing back. If it happens often, it is called reflux disease.
108274.m: Stomach contents flowing back is called reflux.

108275.e: Fatty food stays in the stomach for a long time and can loosen the sphincter to the oesophagus. Spicy food, coffee and chocolate can also cause problems.
108275.m: Very fatty food can trigger heartburn.

108276.q: Why does raising the upper body in bed help against heartburn at night?
a: The stomach then makes no acid
108276.e: If the upper body is higher, the acid has to rise against gravity. It manages this much less well.
108276.m: A raised upper body makes it harder for acid to rise.

108277.q: Which acid is in stomach acid?
108277.e: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid. It makes the gastric juice strongly acidic.

108278.q: Roughly what pH does the gastric juice in an empty stomach have?
108278.e: With a pH of about 1 to 2, the empty stomach is very acidic. A pH of 7 would be neutral.

108279.q: Which cells in the stomach lining make the acid?
108279.e: The parietal cells sit in the glands of the stomach lining. They release the acid into the inside of the stomach.

108280.q: What protective job does stomach acid do?
108280.e: Many bacteria and other germs do not survive the strong acid. In this way the stomach protects against germs in food.
108280.m: Stomach acid kills many germs in food.

108281.q: Why does stomach acid not digest the stomach wall itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects it
The stomach is made of bone
The stomach wall is made of fat
108281.e: The stomach lining makes a thick layer of mucus. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
108281.m: Mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

108282.q: Which protein-splitting enzyme is activated by stomach acid?
108282.e: The stomach releases an inactive form called pepsinogen. The acid turns it into the active enzyme pepsin.
108282.m: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin.

108283.q: Roughly how much gastric juice does an adult make each day?
108283.e: The stomach lining makes about 2 to 3 litres of gastric juice every day. It contains acid, mucus and enzymes.
108283.m: The stomach makes several litres of gastric juice every day.

108284.q: What does stomach acid do to the proteins in food?
108284.e: The acid destroys the shape of the proteins; they are denatured. Unfolded proteins are easier for enzymes to break down.
108284.m: Stomach acid unfolds proteins for digestion.

108285.q: What can make the stomach produce gastric juice even before you eat?
a: The smell or sight of food
108285.e: Just smelling, seeing or thinking about food stimulates gastric juice through the nerves. The stomach gets ready for the meal in this way.
108285.m: Even the smell of food gets the stomach going.

a: Wave-like muscle movements in the digestive tract
108286.e: In peristalsis, the muscles of the digestive tract contract in waves. This pushes the contents along bit by bit.
108286.m: Peristalsis pushes food through the body in waves.

108287.q: Why can you swallow even when doing a handstand?
a: The stomach sucks the food in
The tongue pushes it all the way to the stomach
108287.e: The muscles of the oesophagus contract in waves. This movement works even against gravity.
108287.m: Thanks to muscle waves, swallowing works even upside down.

108288.q: Which two muscle layers work together in peristalsis?
108288.e: Circular muscles squeeze the gut, longitudinal muscles shorten it. Together they create a continuous wave.
108288.m: Circular and longitudinal muscles create peristalsis.

108289.q: What is the gut's own network of nerves sometimes called?
108289.e: There are many millions of nerve cells in the gut wall. They control the gut's movements on their own and are therefore also called the belly brain or second brain.
108289.m: The gut has its own nervous system.

108290.q: Where do the rumbling and gurgling noises in your tummy come from?
a: Gut movements push gas and liquid along
The ribs rub against each other
The heart beats against the stomach
108290.e: The muscles of the stomach and gut move gas and liquid along. This creates noises, especially when the stomach is nearly empty.
108290.m: Tummy rumbling comes from the movement of the stomach and gut.

108291.q: What is a dangerous condition called in which the contents of the gut can no longer move on?
108291.e: In a bowel obstruction, the gut is blocked or paralysed. It is an emergency that must be treated quickly in hospital.
108291.m: A bowel obstruction is a medical emergency.

108292.q: What happens to the stomach contents when you are sick?
a: They flow into the large intestine
108292.e: When you vomit, the stomach muscles and the diaphragm contract strongly. The stomach contents are pushed upwards, against the normal direction.
108292.m: When you vomit, transport runs in the wrong direction.

108293.q: Roughly how long does a mouthful take to travel down the oesophagus to the stomach?
108293.e: The oesophagus is about 25 centimetres long. The muscle wave carries a mouthful into the stomach in a few seconds.
108293.m: A mouthful reaches the stomach after a few seconds.

108294.q: Which type of muscle moves the gut without us deciding to?
108294.e: The gut wall is made of smooth muscle. It works by itself, without us controlling it consciously.
108294.m: Smooth muscles move the gut without our help.

108591.q: Which organ is the body's most important detox centre?
108591.e: The liver breaks down many toxins, medicines and alcohol or makes them harmless. Afterwards they can be got rid of via the kidneys or the bile.
108591.m: The liver is the body's great detox centre.

108592.q: Into which substance does the liver turn the toxic ammonia from breaking down protein?
108592.e: Breaking down protein produces toxic ammonia. The liver turns it into harmless urea, which the kidneys remove in urine.
108592.m: The liver turns toxic ammonia into harmless urea.

108593.q: To which organ does blood from the gut flow first, so that absorbed substances can be checked?
108593.e: The nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and gut flows first to the liver. It processes the substances and makes toxic ones harmless.
108593.m: Blood from the gut flows to the liver first.

108594.q: What helps alcohol in the blood to be broken down faster?
a: Nothing, the liver simply needs time
108594.e: The liver breaks down alcohol slowly and steadily. Coffee, showers or fresh air do not speed this up.
108594.m: Alcohol is broken down only slowly, and nothing can speed up the liver.

108595.q: Which liquid does the liver make, which it also uses to send waste substances into the gut?
108595.e: The liver makes bile every day. With it, waste substances get into the gut, and bile also helps to digest fat.
108595.m: Bile carries waste substances from the liver into the gut.

108596.q: Where is bile stored before it flows into the gut?
108596.e: The gall bladder lies on the underside of the liver. It stores and concentrates the bile and releases it into the duodenum after a fatty meal.
108596.m: The gall bladder stores the bile that the liver makes.

108597.q: Which liver disease often results from years of heavy drinking and scars the organ?
108597.e: In cirrhosis, healthy liver tissue is gradually replaced by scar tissue. The liver can then do its jobs, including detoxifying, less and less well.
108597.m: Too much alcohol can permanently scar the liver.

108598.q: What special ability does the liver have compared with many other organs?
108598.e: The liver regenerates well: if part of it is removed, the remaining tissue grows back. That is why a living person can even donate part of their liver.
108598.m: The liver can regrow lost tissue.

108599.q: Where in the body is the liver?
a: In the upper right of the belly
In the lower left of the belly
108599.e: The liver lies in the upper right of the belly, directly below the diaphragm. It is partly protected by the ribs.
108599.m: The liver lies in the upper right of the belly below the diaphragm.

108600.e: Glycogen is a polysaccharide, which means it is built from a great many sugar units. Humans and animals use it to store sugar as a quick energy reserve.
108600.m: Glycogen is the sugar store of humans and animals.

108601.q: In which two tissues do humans store the most glycogen?
108601.e: The liver and the skeletal muscles contain most of the glycogen. Because there is so much muscle, the muscles even store more in total than the liver.
108601.m: The liver and muscles are the big glycogen stores.

108602.q: What building blocks is glycogen made of?
108602.e: Glycogen is a long, highly branched chain of glucose molecules. When needed, single glucose units are split off again.
108602.m: Glycogen is made of many glucose units.

108603.q: Which hormone makes sure that sugar is stored as glycogen after a meal?
108603.e: After a meal, blood sugar rises and the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin helps the liver and muscles take in glucose and store it as glycogen.
108603.m: Insulin makes sugar be stored as glycogen.

108604.q: Which hormone makes the liver break down glycogen when blood sugar is too low?
108604.e: Glucagon is also made in the pancreas. It makes the liver split glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
108604.m: Glucagon takes sugar out of the liver's glycogen store.

108605.q: What does a muscle use its own glycogen for?
108605.e: Muscle glycogen mainly serves as energy for the muscle itself during movement. The liver, on the other hand, releases glucose from its glycogen into the blood and so supplies the whole body.
108605.m: Muscles use their glycogen mainly for themselves.

108606.q: Which storage substance made from glucose do plants form instead of glycogen?
108606.e: Plants store sugar as starch, for example in potatoes or cereal grains.
108606.m: Plants store sugar as starch, animals as glycogen.

108607.q: Why do endurance athletes like to eat pasta before a competition?
108607.e: Pasta contains a lot of starch, which is digested into glucose. From this the body fills up its glycogen stores in the muscles and liver, which are used up quickly in endurance sport.
108607.m: Carbohydrates fill the glycogen stores for sport.

108608.q: What is glycogen also called because it resembles the storage substance of plants?
108608.e: Glycogen is built similarly to plant starch, only more branched. That is why it is often called animal starch.
108608.m: Glycogen is also called animal starch.

108609.q: What does the word hepatitis mean?
108609.e: The Greek word “hepar” means liver, and the ending “-itis” stands for inflammation. So hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver.
108609.m: Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver.

108610.q: What is the most common cause of hepatitis?
108610.e: Hepatitis is most often caused by hepatitis viruses. The main types are A, B, C, D and E.
108610.m: Most cases of liver inflammation are caused by viruses.

108611.q: How do people usually catch hepatitis A?
108611.e: Hepatitis A viruses leave the body in poo and can be passed on through contaminated drinking water or food. Washing your hands thoroughly protects you.
108611.m: Thorough hand washing protects against hepatitis A.

108612.q: How are the hepatitis B and C viruses mainly passed on?
108612.e: These viruses pass from person to person mainly through blood, for example through shared needles. That is why hospitals use sterile single-use needles.
108612.m: Hepatitis B and C are mainly passed on through blood.

108613.q: Against which forms of hepatitis is there a vaccine?
108613.e: There are effective vaccines against hepatitis A and hepatitis B. There is no vaccine against hepatitis C yet, but there are good medicines.
108613.m: You can be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B.

108614.q: A case of hepatitis does not heal and lasts for years. What is such a long-lasting illness called?
108614.e: An illness is called chronic if it lasts a long time or keeps coming back. An acute illness starts suddenly and is usually over after a short time. Hepatitis C often becomes chronic.
108614.m: A chronic illness lasts a very long time.

108615.q: Which sign can appear with hepatitis?
108615.e: If the liver is inflamed, it can no longer break down the yellow pigment bilirubin properly. It settles in the skin and eyes; this is called jaundice.
108615.m: With an inflamed liver, the skin and eyes can turn yellow.

108616.q: What is the best way to protect yourself against hepatitis B?
108616.e: There is an effective vaccine against hepatitis B, which is recommended for teenagers in Switzerland. It also protects against hepatitis D at the same time.
108616.m: A vaccine protects against hepatitis B.

108617.q: Which job of the liver can be disturbed by hepatitis?
a: It breaks down toxins in the body
108617.e: The liver is the most important detox organ. It breaks down alcohol and medicines, for example. If it is inflamed, it works less well.

108618.q: Which parts of the body turn yellow with jaundice?
a: The skin and the whites of the eyes
108618.e: In jaundice, a yellow pigment builds up in the tissues. It is often seen first in the whites of the eyes, then in the skin.
108618.m: With jaundice, the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow.

108619.q: What causes the yellow colour in jaundice?
a: A yellow waste substance in the blood
108619.e: When red blood cells are broken down, a yellow substance called bilirubin is made. If the liver cannot remove it fast enough, it settles in the skin and eyes.
108619.m: In jaundice, a yellow waste substance in the blood colours the skin.

108620.q: What is bilirubin made from in the body?
108620.e: Red blood cells live for about 120 days. When their pigment haemoglobin is broken down, bilirubin is made, which the liver processes further.
108620.m: Bilirubin comes from breaking down red blood pigment.

108621.q: Which organ is often ill when someone has jaundice?
108621.e: The liver processes the yellow waste substance from the blood. If it is ill, the substance builds up and the skin and eyes turn yellow.
108621.m: Jaundice often points to a problem with the liver.

108622.q: How is the common jaundice of newborn babies often treated?
a: With a brace on the teeth
108622.e: Newborn babies often have mild jaundice. If it is stronger, blue light helps to break down the bilirubin in the skin.
108622.m: Blue light helps against jaundice in newborn babies.

108623.q: What can block the bile duct and so cause jaundice?
108623.e: A gallstone can block the flow of bile into the gut. The bilirubin then backs up into the blood and jaundice develops.
108623.m: A blocked bile duct can cause jaundice.

108624.q: How does urine often change in jaundice caused by liver disease?
108624.e: When there is a lot of bilirubin in the blood, the kidneys get rid of some of it. The urine then turns dark, often like dark beer, while the poo can become pale.
108624.m: With jaundice, the urine can turn dark.

108625.q: Why is jaundice so common in newborn babies in their first days of life?
a: Their liver is not yet fully mature.
They lie in the sun too much.
108625.e: Newborn babies break down many red blood cells after birth. At first, their immature liver cannot process the resulting bilirubin fast enough.
108625.m: A newborn baby's liver first has to get up to speed.

108626.e: The ureter is a thin tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. It runs downwards along the back wall of the belly.
108626.m: The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder.

108627.q: How many ureters does a person normally have?
108627.e: Each of the two kidneys has a ureter. Both lead into the one bladder.
108627.m: Each kidney has its own ureter.

108628.q: Roughly how long is a ureter in an adult?
108628.e: The ureter runs from the renal pelvis along the back wall of the belly down into the lower pelvis. In adults it is about 25 to 30 cm long.
108628.m: A ureter is about as long as a school ruler.

108629.q: How is urine moved through the ureter?
108629.e: The wall of the ureter contains muscles that contract in waves. This movement is called peristalsis and pushes urine into the bladder even when you are lying down.
108629.m: Muscle waves push urine through the ureter.

108630.q: Roughly how wide is a ureter in an adult?
108630.e: The ureter is a narrow muscular tube with a diameter of about 4 to 7 mm. That is why even small stones can get stuck in it.
108630.m: The ureter is only a few millimetres wide.

108631.q: Which of these is NOT part of the urinary tract?
108631.e: The urinary tract includes the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and urethra. The oesophagus belongs to the digestive system.
108631.m: The ureters, bladder and urethra make up the urinary tract.

108632.q: Why does urine normally not flow back from the bladder into the ureter?
a: The opening works like a valve.
108632.e: The ureter passes at a slant through the bladder wall. When the bladder fills, it presses this spot shut so that it works like a valve.
108632.m: A valve at the bladder stops urine flowing back.

108633.q: Why can kidney stones get stuck in the ureter?
a: The ureter is only a few millimetres wide
The ureter is filled with hair
108633.e: The ureter is a narrow tube and especially thin in a few places. A stone can get stuck there and cause severe pain.
108633.m: Kidney stones can get stuck in the narrow ureter.

108634.q: What job does the bladder do?
108634.e: The kidneys make urine all the time. The bladder collects it so that we do not have to go to the toilet constantly.
108634.m: The bladder collects urine until we go to the toilet.

108635.e: The bladder lies in the lower belly in the pelvis, behind the pubic bone. There it is protected by the pelvic bones.
108635.m: The bladder lies protected in the lower pelvis.

108636.q: What do we feel when the bladder fills up?
108636.e: There are stretch sensors in the bladder wall. When the bladder is quite full, they report this to the brain and we feel the urge to wee.
108636.m: A full bladder makes itself felt with the urge to wee.

108637.q: What is the muscle called that closes the bladder?
108637.e: A sphincter muscle keeps the bladder exit closed. When you wee, it relaxes and the urine can flow out.
108637.m: A sphincter keeps the bladder closed.

108638.q: What usually causes a bladder infection?
108638.e: In a bladder infection, bacteria have usually got into the bladder. A burning feeling when weeing and needing to go often are typical.
108638.m: A bladder infection is usually caused by bacteria.

108639.q: What is it called when someone cannot hold in their urine?
108639.e: Incontinence means that urine leaks out without the person wanting it to. It is more common in older people and can often be improved with pelvic floor exercises.
108639.m: Someone who cannot hold in urine has incontinence.

108640.q: Why can the bladder stretch a lot?
a: Its wall is stretchy and folded.
108640.e: The bladder wall is made of muscle and a special, folded lining. As it fills, the folds smooth out and the bladder gets bigger.
108640.m: The bladder is a stretchy muscular bag.

108641.q: Where does urine flow when it leaves the bladder?
108641.e: When you wee, urine leaves the bladder through the urethra to the outside. The ureters, on the other hand, carry urine from the kidneys into the bladder.
108641.m: Urine flows out of the bladder through the urethra.

108642.q: What does the muscle in the bladder wall do when you wee?
a: It contracts and squeezes the urine out
It relaxes and holds the urine back
108642.e: The bladder wall is mostly made of muscle. When you wee, it contracts while the sphincter opens.
108642.m: The bladder muscle squeezes the urine out when you wee.

108643.q: What is urine mostly made of?
108643.e: Urine is about 95 per cent water. Salts and various waste substances are dissolved in it.

108644.q: Which dissolved waste substance is found most in urine?
108644.e: Urea is the most important dissolved waste substance that the kidneys get rid of in urine.
108644.m: Urea is the main waste substance in urine.

108645.q: Roughly how much urine does a healthy adult pass each day?
108645.e: A healthy adult passes about 1.5 litres of urine a day. The amount depends a lot on how much you drink and sweat.
108645.m: An adult passes about one and a half litres of urine a day.

108646.q: What does very dark yellow urine often show?
a: That you have drunk too little
That you have slept too much
That you have laughed too much
108646.e: If you drink little, the kidneys save water and the urine becomes more concentrated and darker. Pale yellow urine usually shows that you are drinking enough.
108646.m: Pale urine usually shows that you have drunk enough.

108647.q: Which illness can sugar in the urine point to?
108647.e: Normally the kidneys take all the sugar back into the blood. If blood sugar is too high, as in diabetes, they cannot manage this, and sugar gets into the urine.
108647.m: Sugar in the urine can be a sign of diabetes.

108648.q: What can a doctor use to quickly test urine for sugar, blood or protein?
108648.e: A urine test strip has small test pads that change colour with certain substances. This gives first clues to illnesses in a short time.
108648.m: A test strip shows substances in urine by changing colour.

108649.q: In which check in top-level sport is urine often tested?
a: When start numbers are handed out
108649.e: Many banned substances and their breakdown products can be detected in urine. That is why athletes give a urine sample in doping tests.
108649.m: Urine is often tested in doping controls.

108650.q: What is the urine that the kidneys finally pass out called, as opposed to primary urine?
108650.e: The kidneys first filter a great deal of primary urine from the blood. After water and nutrients are taken back, the much smaller amount of final urine is left.
108650.m: The urine that leaves the body is called final urine.

108651.e: Kidney stones form when dissolved substances in urine clump together into crystals. They can be as small as sand or bigger than a pea.
108651.m: Kidney stones are made of crystals of substances in urine.

108652.q: How big can kidney stones be?
a: From as tiny as sand to bigger than a pea
Always exactly the size of an apple
Only the size of an atom
108652.e: Kidney stones form from crystals in urine. Some are as tiny as grains of sand, others grow over years and get bigger than a pea.
108652.m: Kidney stones can be very small or quite large.

108653.q: What is an important way to prevent kidney stones?
108653.e: If you drink plenty, your urine is diluted. Then the substances are less likely to clump together into crystals.
108653.m: Drinking plenty protects against kidney stones.

108654.q: What is the severe pain called that a moving kidney stone can cause?
108654.e: If a stone moves into the ureter, urine backs up and the muscles cramp. The pain comes in waves and is among the worst there is.
108654.m: A moving kidney stone can cause renal colic.

108655.q: What can be used to break up kidney stones from outside the body?
108655.e: In shock wave therapy, focused pressure waves are aimed at the stone from outside. It breaks into small pieces that leave the body in urine.
108655.m: Shock waves can break up kidney stones.

108656.q: What often happens to a very small kidney stone?
a: It passes out with the urine.
108656.e: Small stones of a few millimetres are often flushed out with the urine. Drinking plenty and moving about can help.
108656.m: Small kidney stones often pass by themselves.

108657.e: Urinary stones usually form in the kidney and can move into the ureter or bladder. That is why they are also called urinary stones in general.
108657.m: Kidney stones form in the urinary tract.

108658.q: Why do hot summer days make kidney stones more likely?
a: You sweat a lot and the urine becomes concentrated.
You eat more ice cream with stones in it.
108658.e: In the heat, the body loses a lot of water through sweat. If you do not drink enough to make up for it, your urine is concentrated and crystals form more easily.
108658.m: In hot weather you must drink more to prevent kidney stones.

108659.e: In dialysis, waste substances and extra water are removed from the blood. In this way it does the work of diseased kidneys.
108659.m: Dialysis cleans the blood when the kidneys fail.

108660.q: When does a person need dialysis?
a: When the kidneys hardly work any more
108660.e: In severe kidney failure, toxins and water build up in the body. Without dialysis or a new kidney, this would be life-threatening.
108660.m: With kidney failure, you need dialysis or a new kidney.

108661.q: What is the machine for cleaning the blood often called in everyday language?
108661.e: The dialysis machine takes over the filtering work of the kidney. That is why it is often called an artificial kidney.
108661.m: The dialysis machine is called an artificial kidney.

108662.q: How often a week do many people go for haemodialysis?
108662.e: Haemodialysis is usually done three times a week and lasts about four to five hours each time. It takes a lot of time and patience.
108662.m: Haemodialysis usually takes place three times a week.

108663.q: What separates the blood from the cleaning fluid in a dialysis machine?
108663.e: The membrane has tiny pores. Small waste substances pass through into the cleaning fluid, while blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
108663.m: In dialysis, a fine membrane filters the blood.

108664.q: Which membrane in the body acts as a filter in peritoneal dialysis?
108664.e: In peritoneal dialysis, cleaning fluid is put into the belly. The peritoneum, which has a good blood supply, then works as a filter, and this can even be done at home.
108664.m: In peritoneal dialysis, your own peritoneum does the filtering.

108665.q: What can allow a person with diseased kidneys to live without dialysis?
108665.e: If someone receives a healthy donor kidney, it takes over cleaning the blood. Then dialysis is no longer needed.
108665.m: A new kidney can replace dialysis.

108666.q: Why do dialysis patients often have to watch exactly how much they drink?
a: Their kidneys hardly get rid of any water.
108666.e: Diseased kidneys often make almost no urine any more. Water they drink stays in the body until it is removed at the next dialysis.
108666.m: Without healthy kidneys, you have to ration how much you drink.

108667.e: In a kidney transplant, a person with kidney failure receives a kidney from a donor. The new kidney then does the work of the diseased kidneys.
108667.m: In a transplant, you receive a donated kidney.

108668.q: Why can a healthy person donate a kidney while still alive?
a: You can live well with one kidney.
108668.e: One healthy kidney can largely do the work of both kidneys. That is why family members often donate a kidney to someone who is ill.
108668.m: You can live well with one healthy kidney.

108669.q: Who can a donor kidney come from?
a: From a living person or a person who has died
108669.e: Kidneys can be donated by people who have died. Because you can live well with one kidney, living people donate too, often family members.
108669.m: Donor kidneys come from living people or people who have died.

108670.q: Why do people with a donated kidney take medicines that suppress the immune system?
a: So the body does not reject the kidney
108670.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ and would attack it. Medicines that dampen the immune system prevent this rejection.
108670.m: Medicines stop the body rejecting a foreign kidney.

108671.q: Which organ is transplanted most often worldwide?
108671.e: The kidney is the organ transplanted most often. Many people with kidney failure are waiting for a donor organ.
108671.m: The kidney is the organ transplanted most often.

108672.q: What does the opt-out system for organ donation in Switzerland mean?
a: Anyone who has not objected counts as a donor
Nobody is allowed to donate organs
Everyone must sign a contract to donate
108672.e: In 2022, voters said yes to the extended opt-out system. Anyone who has not objected during their lifetime counts as a donor, but their relatives are still involved.
108672.m: In an opt-out system, you must say no if you do not want to donate.

108673.q: What is the national foundation called that coordinates the allocation of donor organs in Switzerland?
108673.e: Swisstransplant keeps the waiting list and coordinates the allocation of donor organs in Switzerland. It works together with the transplant centres.
108673.m: Swisstransplant coordinates organ donation in Switzerland.

108674.q: What often happens to a person's own diseased kidneys in a kidney transplant?
a: They usually stay in the body.
They are always given away for donation.
108674.e: The new kidney is usually placed in the lower belly. The person's own kidneys are often not removed, so the person then has three kidneys.
108674.m: After a transplant, people often have three kidneys in their body.

a: The smallest working unit of the kidney
108675.e: A nephron is a tiny filter unit in which urine is made from blood. Only millions of these nephrons together give the kidneys their full power.
108675.m: The nephron is the smallest working unit of the kidney.

108676.q: Roughly how many nephrons does a human kidney contain?
108676.e: Each kidney has around a million nephrons. So both kidneys together have about two million of these filter units.
108676.m: Each kidney has around a million nephrons.

108677.q: What is made in the nephrons of the kidney?
108677.e: The blood is filtered in the nephrons. From this, urine is made step by step.
108677.m: Urine is made in the nephrons.

108678.q: What happens if many nephrons in a kidney are destroyed?
a: The kidney can no longer clean the blood well
The kidney gets bigger and stronger
108678.e: If many nephrons stop working, waste substances stay in the blood. In severe kidney failure, blood cleaning (dialysis) or a donor kidney is needed.
108678.m: Without enough nephrons, the kidney cannot clean the blood.

108679.q: Roughly how much primary urine do an adult's kidneys filter each day?
108679.e: Every day the kidneys filter around 180 litres of primary urine from the blood. They take back over 99 per cent of it, so only a small remainder is passed out.
108679.m: The kidneys filter around 180 litres of primary urine every day.

108680.q: Why is urine often darker in the morning than during the day?
a: The kidney saves water at night, so the urine is more concentrated
You drank too much at night
The light in the bedroom colours it
The kidney rests completely at night
108680.e: At night you drink nothing. So the nephrons take more water back into the blood, and the urine becomes more concentrated and darker.
108680.m: Little water in the body makes urine darker.

108681.q: Which valuable substances do the tubules of the nephron take back from the primary urine into the blood?
108681.e: In the kidney tubules, water, glucose and many salts are taken back into the blood. Waste substances such as urea mostly stay in the urine.
108681.m: The nephron takes water, sugar and salts back into the blood.

108682.q: What does the kidney do if you have drunk too little on a hot day?
a: It saves water and makes less urine
It makes a lot of pale urine
It gives water to the stomach
108682.e: When water is short, a hormone makes the kidney take more water back into the blood. A small amount of dark urine is made.
108682.m: When water is short, the kidney saves water.

108683.q: What job does the renal pelvis do?
108683.e: In the renal pelvis, the finished urine from all parts of the kidney flows together. From there it flows on towards the bladder.
108683.m: The renal pelvis collects urine before it flows on.

108684.q: Where does urine flow from the renal pelvis?
108684.e: The renal pelvis narrows like a funnel and leads into the ureter. This carries the urine to the bladder.
108684.m: From the renal pelvis, urine flows into the ureter.

108685.q: Where does the ureter carry urine from the renal pelvis to?
108685.e: The ureter is a thin tube. It carries urine from the renal pelvis into the bladder, where it is collected.
108685.m: The ureter carries urine to the bladder.

108686.q: What are typical signs of a kidney infection?
a: Fever and pain in the side
108686.e: In a kidney infection, bacteria usually travel up from the bladder. Fever and pain at the side of the back are typical; it is treated with antibiotics.
108686.m: A kidney infection must be treated by a doctor.

108687.q: On which side of the bean-shaped kidney is the renal pelvis?
a: At the dent facing the spine
On the outside facing the back
108687.e: The kidney has a dent on its inner side, the hilum. Blood vessels go in and out there, and the renal pelvis is there too.
108687.m: The renal pelvis lies at the dent of the kidney.

108688.q: What shape is a human kidney?
108688.e: The kidney is bean-shaped and about as big as a fist. The kidneys lie to the left and right of the spine in the back.
108688.m: The kidney is shaped like a bean.

108689.q: What happens if the outflow from the renal pelvis is permanently blocked?
a: Urine backs up in the kidney.
The liver takes over the urine.
108689.e: If the outflow is blocked, for example by a stone, urine backs up and the renal pelvis widens. Without treatment, the kidney can be damaged.
108689.m: A blocked outflow makes urine back up into the kidney.

108690.q: The kidney has an outer and an inner layer. What is the outer one called?
108690.e: The renal cortex is on the outside, the renal medulla on the inside. Right in the middle, the renal pelvis collects the urine.
108690.m: The outer layer of the kidney is the renal cortex.

108986.q: Which simple sugar is carried in the blood to the cells and is their most important source of energy?
108986.e: Glucose, also called grape sugar, is blood sugar. The cells get energy from it.
108986.m: Glucose is the sugar that reaches the cells in the blood.

108987.q: In which form do plants such as the potato store their carbohydrates?
108987.e: Plants link many glucose units together to form starch and store it in tubers, grains and seeds.
108987.m: Potatoes, rice and cereals are rich in starch.

108988.q: What is the double sugar made of two glucose units called, which forms in germinating grain for malt?
108988.e: Maltose is also called malt sugar. It forms when germinating grain breaks down its starch.

108989.q: What is the sugar called that is found naturally in milk?
108989.e: Lactose is also called milk sugar. People with lactose intolerance find it hard to digest.

108990.q: From which plant do the sugar factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld make household sugar?
108990.e: In Switzerland, sugar is made from sugar beet grown in Swiss fields. Sugar cane only grows in warm countries.
108990.m: Swiss sugar comes from sugar beet.

108991.q: Which food makes blood sugar rise especially quickly?
108991.e: Glucose goes straight into the blood without needing to be digested. Thanks to their fibre, wholegrains, lentils and nuts make blood sugar rise slowly.
108991.m: Glucose gets into the blood very quickly.

108992.q: Roughly how much energy does 1 gram of carbohydrate provide?
108992.e: One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal or 17 kJ. One gram of protein provides the same amount.
108992.m: One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kilocalories.

108993.q: According to dietary recommendations, roughly what share of daily energy should carbohydrates provide?
108993.e: It is recommended that about half of your energy comes from carbohydrates, ideally from wholegrains, potatoes, pulses and fruit.
108993.m: Carbohydrates are the biggest source of energy in the diet.

108994.q: Which sugar is found mainly in fruit and honey?
108994.e: Fructose is also called fruit sugar. It is sweeter than household sugar.

108995.q: What building blocks are proteins made of?
108995.e: Proteins are long chains of amino acids. The order of the amino acids decides the shape and job of the protein.
108995.m: Proteins are made of amino acids.

108996.q: What does it mean when an amino acid is “essential”?
a: The body cannot make it itself
It is found only in meat
It provides especially lots of energy
It is poisonous in large amounts
108996.e: Essential amino acids must come from food, because the body cannot make them.
108996.m: Essential amino acids must come from food.

108997.q: Which foods are good plant sources of protein?
108997.e: Lentils, beans, peas and chickpeas contain a lot of protein. Salad, fruit and oil provide hardly any protein.
108997.m: Pulses are rich in plant protein.

108998.q: In which organ does the enzyme pepsin start digesting protein?
108998.e: Stomach acid makes proteins swell, and pepsin breaks them into shorter pieces. Digestion continues in the small intestine.
108998.m: Protein digestion begins in the stomach.

108999.q: Which protein are hair and fingernails mainly made of?
108999.e: Keratin is a tough fibrous protein. It is also found in horns, feathers and the top layer of the skin.
108999.m: Hair and nails are made of keratin.

109000.q: What does the body mainly need protein for?
109000.e: Proteins are the body's building materials. Muscles, skin, hair and many other parts of the cells are made from them.
109000.m: Protein is the building material for muscles and cells.

109001.q: What job do enzymes, which are mostly proteins, do?
109001.e: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they make chemical reactions in the body happen quickly, for example in digestion.
109001.m: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions in the body.

109002.q: What can happen to children with a severe lack of protein?
a: They grow poorly and become weak
109002.e: Without enough protein, the body lacks building materials. Children then grow poorly, become weak and are often ill.
109002.m: Children need enough protein to grow.

109003.q: A yoghurt contains 4 g of protein per 100 g. How much protein is in a 180 g pot?
109003.e: You calculate 4 g times 1.8, because 180 divided by 100 is 1.8. That makes 7.2 g of protein.
109003.m: Convert nutrition values per 100 g using the amount in the pack.

109004.q: Which of these vitamins is fat-soluble?
109004.e: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat. Vitamin C, on the other hand, dissolves in water.
109004.m: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

109005.q: What does the body need fat from food for?
a: As an energy store and to absorb certain vitamins
To carry oxygen in the blood
109005.e: Fat provides a lot of energy and is stored as a reserve. The body also needs fat to absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.
109005.m: Fat provides energy and helps absorb vitamins.

109006.q: Which fatty acids are especially common in butter and make it solid at room temperature?
109006.e: Saturated fatty acids have straight chains that pack closely together. That is why animal fats such as butter tend to be solid and oils tend to be liquid.
109006.m: Saturated fatty acids make fats solid.

109007.q: Which food is especially rich in omega-3 fatty acids?
109007.e: Oily sea fish such as salmon, herring or mackerel contain a lot of omega-3 fatty acids. They are important for the heart and brain.
109007.m: Oily fish provides lots of omega-3 fatty acids.

109008.q: Which body fluid breaks fat in the gut into fine droplets so that it is digested better?
109008.e: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It emulsifies fat so that enzymes can break it down more easily.

109009.q: Which fats are considered especially unhealthy, partly because they form when oils are hardened industrially?
109009.e: Trans fatty acids raise the unhealthy LDL cholesterol. Switzerland limits their amount in cooking oils and fats by law.
109009.m: Trans fats are bad for the heart and blood vessels.

109010.q: Besides storing energy, what job does the fatty tissue under the skin do?
109010.e: The fat under the skin insulates the body against heat loss and cushions it against knocks.
109010.m: Fat under the skin keeps you warm and cushions the body.

109011.q: What happens to most fibre in the small intestine?
109011.e: Humans lack the enzymes to break down fibre. So it moves on into the large intestine.

109012.q: Which type of fibre forms the cell walls of plants?
109012.e: Cellulose is the most common plant substance and gives plant cells their strength. Paper and cotton are also mostly made of it.
109012.m: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose.

109013.q: According to recommendations, how much fibre should adults eat at least each day?
109013.e: At least about 30 g a day is recommended. Many people eat much less.
109013.m: Adults should eat about 30 grams of fibre a day.

109014.q: Which bread contains the most fibre?
109014.e: For wholemeal bread, the whole grain is ground including its outer layers. That is exactly where most of the fibre is.
109014.m: Wholegrain products contain lots of fibre.

109015.q: Which fibre from apples and quinces makes jam and jelly set?
109015.e: Pectin is a soluble fibre from the cell walls of fruit. With sugar and acid it forms a gel.
109015.m: Pectin from fruit makes jam set.

109016.q: Why should you drink enough when eating a high-fibre diet?
a: Because fibre binds water and swells
Because it draws salt out of the body
Because it raises the pulse a lot
Because it makes acid in the stomach
109016.e: Fibre soaks up water and so increases the volume of the gut contents. Without enough fluid, constipation can result.
109016.m: If you eat lots of fibre, you should drink plenty.

109017.q: What breaks down some of the fibre in the large intestine?
109017.e: Bacteria in the large intestine ferment certain kinds of fibre. This produces substances that are good for the gut lining, but also gases.

109018.q: What are the outer layers of the cereal grain called, which are separated during milling and contain lots of fibre?
109018.e: Bran is made of the husk and outer layers of the grain. You can mix it into muesli, for example.

109019.q: How does fibre affect the feeling of being full?
a: It keeps you full for longer
109019.e: High-fibre food has to be chewed for longer, fills the stomach and makes blood sugar rise more slowly. That is why the full feeling lasts longer.
109019.m: Fibre keeps you full for a long time.

109020.q: Which mineral is the main building block of bones and teeth and is found in large amounts in milk?
109020.e: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard. Dairy products such as cheese and yoghurt are good sources of calcium.
109020.m: Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

109021.q: Chemically, table salt is made of sodium and which other substance?
109021.e: Table salt is sodium chloride, with the formula NaCl. It provides the body with sodium and chloride.

109022.q: According to the World Health Organization, what is the most salt adults should eat per day?
109022.e: The WHO recommends less than 5 g of salt a day, about a teaspoon. In Switzerland, people eat much more on average.
109022.m: You should not eat more than 5 grams of salt a day.

109023.q: Which mineral sits at the centre of the green leaf pigment chlorophyll?
109023.e: Every chlorophyll molecule contains a magnesium atom in its centre. That is why green leafy vegetables such as spinach are a good source of magnesium.
109023.m: There is magnesium in the green of leaves.

109024.q: What makes major minerals such as calcium different from trace elements?
a: The body contains more of them
They provide a lot of energy
They are found only in meat
109024.e: Major minerals are found in the body in larger amounts, trace elements only in tiny traces. Both must be taken in with food.
109024.m: The body contains larger amounts of major minerals than of trace elements.

109025.q: Which vitamin does the gut need to absorb calcium well?
109025.e: Vitamin D helps calcium be absorbed from the gut. The skin makes it with the help of sunlight.
109025.m: Without vitamin D, the body absorbs little calcium.

109026.q: Which mineral do you lose especially when you sweat?
109026.e: Sweat tastes salty because it contains sodium chloride. During long sport, you may therefore need to replace salt as well.
109026.m: Sweating mainly makes you lose sodium.

109027.q: Which mineral is important for relaxing the muscles and is often taken for calf cramps?
109027.e: Magnesium plays a part in muscle relaxation and in passing signals along nerves. It is found in nuts, wholegrains and green vegetables.

109028.q: Which gland grows larger when there is a lack of iodine and forms a goitre?
109028.e: The thyroid gland needs iodine for its hormones. If iodine is missing, the gland grows to catch more iodine, and a goitre forms.
109028.m: A lack of iodine makes the thyroid gland grow.

109029.q: Why is iodine added to table salt in Switzerland?
a: Because the soil and food contain little iodine
109029.e: The soils in the Alps are low in iodine. In the past, many people therefore suffered from a lack of iodine and goitre. Iodised salt has been available in Switzerland since 1922.
109029.m: Iodised salt protects against a lack of iodine.

109030.q: Which trace element is contained in the red blood pigment haemoglobin?
109030.e: In haemoglobin, an iron atom binds the oxygen. This is how the blood can carry oxygen.
109030.m: The blood needs iron to carry oxygen.

109031.q: What is a common result of a lack of iron?
109031.e: Without enough iron, the body makes too little red blood pigment. You become pale, tired and less able to perform.
109031.m: A lack of iron makes you tired and pale.

109032.q: Which metal, also found in electric cables, does the body need as a trace element?
109032.e: Copper is part of important enzymes, for example for making blood. Lead, mercury and cadmium, on the other hand, are poisonous heavy metals.
109032.m: Copper is a vital trace element.

109033.q: Which trace element is found in many toothpastes and protects tooth enamel against decay?
109033.e: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to acids. In Switzerland there is also fluoridated table salt.

109034.q: Which trace element is important for the immune system and wound healing and is found in large amounts in oysters?
109034.e: Zinc is part of many enzymes and supports the immune system and wound healing. Good sources are oysters, meat, cheese and wholegrains.

109035.q: Why are some minerals called “trace elements”?
a: The body needs only tiny amounts of them
They leave traces on the skin
They are found only in animal tracks
They are found only in snow
109035.e: The body needs trace elements such as iron, iodine or zinc only in very small amounts. Even so, they are vital.
109035.m: The body needs trace elements only in the tiniest amounts.

109036.q: Which food is a good natural source of iodine?
109036.e: Sea water contains iodine, so sea fish and seaweed are rich in it. Soils in the Alps, on the other hand, tend to be low in iodine.
109036.m: Sea fish provides lots of iodine.

109037.q: What was the kilocalorie originally defined as?
a: Bringing 1 litre of water to the boil
109037.e: A kilocalorie is the amount of heat that warms 1 kg of water by 1 °C. A calorie is enough for 1 g of water.
109037.m: One kilocalorie warms a litre of water by one degree.

109038.q: 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ. Roughly how many kilojoules are 500 kcal?
109038.e: You calculate 500 times 4.2 and get 2,100 kJ. Exactly, it is 500 times 4.184, which is about 2,092 kJ.
109038.m: To convert kilocalories into kilojoules, multiply by 4.2.

109039.q: What is the official unit of energy that now appears alongside kcal on food packaging?
109039.e: The joule is the SI unit of energy. On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and kilocalories.

109041.q: What do the nutrition values on Swiss food packaging usually refer to?
109041.e: Giving the values per 100 g or 100 ml is required. This makes it easy to compare different products.
109041.m: Nutrition values are given per 100 grams on the pack.

109042.q: What happens if, over a long time, you eat more energy than you use?
109042.e: The body stores extra energy mainly as fat. That is why you put on weight.
109042.m: If you always eat more energy than you use, you put on weight.

109043.q: An apple has about 50 kcal, a slice of cake 350 kcal. How many apples provide as much energy as the cake?
109043.e: You calculate 350 divided by 50 and get 7. So seven apples have as much energy as one slice of cake.
109043.m: Comparing kilocalories shows how energy-rich a food is.

109044.q: Which device is used in the laboratory to find the energy content of a food by burning it?
109044.e: In a calorimeter, the sample is burned and the heat released is measured by how much it warms water.
109044.m: A calorimeter measures energy through the heat produced.

109045.q: What is meant by basal metabolic rate?
109045.e: The basal metabolic rate is the energy the body needs at rest for breathing, heartbeat, body heat and the organs.
109045.m: Even at complete rest, the body uses energy.

109046.q: A rule of thumb says the body needs 1 kcal per kg of body weight per hour at rest. By this rule, what is the basal metabolic rate of a 60 kg person per day?
109046.e: You calculate 60 kg times 24 hours times 1 kcal. That makes 1,440 kcal a day.
109046.m: Basal metabolic rate can be estimated with a simple rule of thumb.

109047.q: What is the extra energy called that the body needs for movement, work and sport?
109047.e: Activity energy expenditure is added to the basal metabolic rate. It is much higher in physically active people.

109048.q: What is the sum of basal metabolic rate and activity energy expenditure called?
109048.e: Total energy expenditure is the whole energy need of a day. Only if you eat that much does your weight stay the same.
109048.m: Basal metabolic rate and activity energy expenditure together make total energy expenditure.

109049.q: How does basal metabolic rate usually change in adults as they get older?
109049.e: With age, muscle mass usually decreases and metabolism slows down. That is why the basal metabolic rate falls.
109049.m: In old age, the body needs less energy at rest.

109050.q: Why do people with a lot of muscle have a higher basal metabolic rate?
a: Muscles use energy even at rest
Muscles store a lot of sugar
109050.e: Muscle tissue is metabolically active and uses energy even when you are sitting or lying down. Fatty tissue, on the other hand, needs little.
109050.m: More muscle means a higher basal metabolic rate.

109051.q: Which organ uses about 20 per cent of the energy at rest, although it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight?
109051.e: The nerve cells in the brain work all the time and need a great deal of energy for this, even during sleep.
109051.m: The brain uses a lot of energy.

109052.q: What makes the basal metabolic rate rise for a while?
109052.e: With a fever, metabolic processes run faster. For every degree of fever, the energy need rises noticeably.
109052.m: A fever increases the body's energy needs.

109053.q: Which sight problem can a lack of vitamin A cause?
109053.e: Without enough vitamin A, the eyes see poorly at dusk. In poor countries this deficiency is still common today.
109053.m: A lack of vitamin A leads to night blindness.

109054.q: Which orange pigment in carrots is a precursor of vitamin A?
109054.e: The body turns beta-carotene into vitamin A when needed. It is also found in pumpkin, apricots and peppers.
109054.m: Beta-carotene is a precursor of vitamin A.

109055.q: Why should you prepare carrots with a little oil or butter?
a: So the vitamin is absorbed better
109055.e: Vitamin A and its precursor are fat-soluble. With a little fat, the gut can absorb them much better.
109055.m: Carrots are best eaten with a little fat.

109056.q: For which sense organ is vitamin A especially important?
109056.e: Vitamin A is needed in the retina for seeing, especially in dim light. Its chemical name, retinol, also reminds us of the retina.
109056.m: Vitamin A is important for the eyes.

109057.q: In which organ does the body store vitamin A, which is why this organ is very rich in it as a food?
109057.e: The liver builds up large stores of vitamin A. So liver as a food contains a great deal of it.

109058.q: Why can too much vitamin A from supplements be harmful?
a: It is stored and builds up
It is removed from the body immediately
109058.e: What the body does not need is not simply passed out in urine but stored. Very large amounts can be poisonous.
109058.m: With vitamin A, too much can do harm.

109059.q: What is the genetically modified rice called that is meant to help against vitamin A deficiency and was partly developed at ETH Zurich?
109059.e: Golden Rice makes a precursor of vitamin A in the grain and is therefore yellowish. It was developed by Ingo Potrykus of ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer.
109059.m: Golden Rice is meant to fight vitamin A deficiency.

109060.q: Which sensory cells in the retina need vitamin A to see at dusk?
109060.e: The rods in the retina are responsible for seeing in dim light. Their visual pigment is made with vitamin A.
109060.m: The rods need vitamin A for seeing at dusk.

109061.q: What makes vitamin B12 in nature?
109061.e: Only microorganisms such as bacteria can make vitamin B12. Animals take it in through their food or from bacteria in their digestive tract.
109061.m: Vitamin B12 is made by bacteria.

109062.q: Which foods mainly contain vitamin B12?
109062.e: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods. Plants provide practically no usable B12.
109062.m: Vitamin B12 is mainly found in animal foods.

109063.q: What can a long-lasting lack of vitamin B12 lead to?
109063.e: Vitamin B12 is needed to make red blood cells and for healthy nerves. A lack leads to anaemia and can permanently damage nerves.
109063.m: A lack of B12 harms the blood and nerves.

109064.q: In which unit is the daily need for vitamin B12 given?
109064.e: The body needs only a few micrograms a day, that is millionths of a gram. Even so, the vitamin is vital.
109064.m: You need only tiny amounts of vitamin B12.

109065.q: Why can some people get a vitamin B12 deficiency despite eating well?
a: Because their body cannot absorb the vitamin properly
Because they drink too much water
Because they are outside too often
109065.e: A special substance from the stomach is needed to absorb vitamin B12. If it is missing or the gut is ill, a deficiency develops even if you eat enough B12.
109065.m: B12 deficiency can also come from poor absorption in the gut.

109066.q: Which group does vitamin B12 belong to?
109066.e: All B vitamins are water-soluble. Vitamin B12 is still an exception, because the body can store larger reserves of it.
109066.m: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin.

109067.q: Why does a vitamin B12 deficiency often show only after years?
a: Because the body has reserves for years
Because B12 only works at night
Because you only need it in old age
Because it is in every vegetable
109067.e: The body stores a few milligrams of vitamin B12. These reserves often last several years before a deficiency appears.
109067.m: B12 deficiency develops slowly because the body has reserves.

109068.q: How is a severe vitamin B12 deficiency often treated when absorption in the gut does not work properly?
109068.e: Injections bypass the gut, so the vitamin goes straight into the blood. The treatment is given by a doctor.

109069.q: A lack of which vitamin causes scurvy?
109069.e: Scurvy develops when the body gets too little vitamin C for weeks. With fresh fruit and vegetables it heals quickly.
109069.m: Scurvy is a vitamin C deficiency disease.

109070.q: Who used to suffer from scurvy especially often?
109070.e: On voyages lasting months there was no fresh fruit or vegetables. Many sailors fell ill or died.

109071.q: Which of these is a typical sign of scurvy?
109071.e: In scurvy, blood vessels and connective tissue become fragile. The gums bleed, wounds heal poorly and teeth can fall out.
109071.m: Bleeding gums are a sign of scurvy.

109072.q: Which remedy worked against scurvy in the ship's doctor James Lind's experiment of 1747?
109072.e: Lind divided sick sailors into groups with different remedies. Only the group with citrus fruit recovered quickly.

109073.q: Which pet, like humans, cannot make the vitamin that protects against scurvy itself?
109073.e: Like humans, guinea pigs lack an enzyme to make this vitamin. That is why they need fresh vegetables every day.
109073.m: Guinea pigs need fresh vegetables every day.

109074.q: Which long-lasting food did the explorer James Cook take on his voyages against scurvy?
109074.e: Sauerkraut keeps for a long time and still contains enough of the protective vitamin. As a result, Cook's crews were largely spared from scurvy.

109075.q: Why is some of the protection against scurvy lost when vegetables are cooked for a long time?
a: The vitamin is sensitive to heat
109075.e: The vitamin is destroyed by heat and oxygen and dissolves into the cooking water. Steaming briefly protects it.

109076.q: Which foods protect especially well against scurvy?
109076.e: Peppers, kiwis, citrus fruit, cabbage and berries contain a lot of the vitamin that protects against scurvy. Cereals, fat and sugar contain hardly any of it.
109076.m: Fresh fruit and vegetables prevent scurvy.

109077.q: Besides meat and fish, what do people who eat a vegan diet also go without?
109077.e: Vegetarians do not eat meat or fish. Vegans leave out all products from animals, so also milk, eggs and honey.
109077.m: Vegan means completely without animal products.

109078.q: Which plant is tofu made from?
109078.e: To make tofu, soya milk is made from soya beans and then made to curdle, similar to making cheese.
109078.m: Tofu is made from soya beans.

109079.q: What is the meat substitute seitan mainly made of?
109079.e: Seitan is made from gluten, the sticky protein in wheat. That is why it is unsuitable for people with coeliac disease.
109079.m: Seitan is made of wheat protein.

109080.q: Which vitamin should people who eat a vegan diet take as a supplement or through fortified foods?
109080.e: Plant foods provide practically no usable vitamin B12. Expert bodies therefore recommend a supplement for vegans.
109080.m: A vegan diet needs a vitamin B12 supplement.

109081.q: Why are many jelly sweets not vegan?
109081.e: Gelatine is made from the skin and bones of animals. Vegan jelly sweets use plant-based gelling agents instead.

109082.q: Which plant ingredient provides lots of omega-3 fatty acids?
109082.e: Linseed, linseed oil, walnuts and algae oil contain omega-3 fatty acids. For vegans they replace fish.
109082.m: Linseed is a plant source of omega-3.

109083.q: Which word was the word “vegan” formed from?
109083.e: The word was formed in England in 1944 from the first and last letters of “vegetarian”.

109084.q: Which of these plant foods is a good source of calcium for vegans?
109084.e: Kale, broccoli, almonds and plant drinks fortified with calcium provide lots of calcium. Cucumbers, rice and apples contain only a little.
109084.m: Green cabbage vegetables provide calcium without milk.

109384.q: How long should you rub in hand sanitiser?
109384.e: The World Health Organization recommends rubbing in the product for 20 to 30 seconds until the hands are dry. This gives the active ingredient enough time to kill the germs.
109384.m: Rub in hand sanitiser for about half a minute.

109385.q: Which active ingredient is in most hand sanitisers?
109385.e: Most hand sanitisers contain alcohols such as ethanol or propanol. These destroy the outer layer of many bacteria and viruses.
109385.m: Alcohol is what makes most hand sanitisers work.

109386.q: What is better when your hands are visibly dirty?
a: Wiping your hands on your trousers
109386.e: Sanitiser does not remove dirt. So visibly dirty hands should be washed with water and soap.
109386.m: Dirty hands need water and soap.

109387.q: Why should you put sanitiser on dry hands?
109387.e: Water on the hands dilutes the product, so it works less well. That is why you should use it on dry hands.
109387.m: Sanitiser works best on dry hands.

109389.q: Against which form of germ do alcohol-based hand sanitisers work poorly?
109389.e: Spores are very tough resting forms of some bacteria. Alcohol hardly kills them, so with such germs you also have to wash your hands.
109389.m: Bacterial spores often survive alcohol unharmed.

109390.q: Which parts of the hand are often forgotten when using sanitiser?
a: The middle of the back of the hand
109390.e: Studies show that thumbs, fingertips and the spaces between the fingers often get too little product. So you should rub these areas in on purpose.
109390.m: When using sanitiser, remember your thumbs and fingertips too.

109391.q: Why do many hand sanitisers contain moisturising additives?
a: So the skin does not dry out
109391.e: Alcohol removes fat and moisture from the skin. Moisturising additives protect the skin, even if you use sanitiser often.
109391.m: Good sanitisers protect the skin with moisturising additives.

109392.q: What is the highest temperature a fridge should be?
109392.e: At no more than about 5 °C, most bacteria multiply only very slowly. The fridge should not be warmer than that.
109392.m: A fridge should be no warmer than about 5 °C.

109393.q: What is it called when germs from raw meat get onto salad via a chopping board?
109393.e: In cross-contamination, germs are carried from one food to another. That is why you use different boards for raw meat and salad.
109393.m: Cut raw meat and salad on separate boards.

109394.q: Where is the safest place to defrost frozen meat?
109394.e: In the fridge, the meat stays cool while defrosting, so bacteria hardly multiply. The thawing liquid is caught and thrown away.
109394.m: Defrost meat slowly in the fridge.

109395.q: In which temperature range do many bacteria in food multiply especially quickly?
109395.e: Between about 5 and 60 °C, many bacteria find good conditions. So warm food should be kept hot or cooled quickly.
109395.m: Keep food hot or cool it quickly.

109396.q: What core temperature should poultry reach at least when it is cooked?
109396.e: Inside the meat, at least 70 °C should be reached. Then germs such as Campylobacter are killed.
109396.m: Cook poultry through until it is at least 70 °C inside.

109397.q: What should you do with bread that has mould growing on it?
a: Scrape off the mould and eat it
109397.e: Moulds spread through soft bread with fine threads that you cannot see. Some produce toxic substances, so the whole loaf belongs in the bin.

109398.q: Why should you wash your hands before cooking?
a: So no germs get into the food
So the pan does not burn
109398.e: There are many germs on your hands. If you wash them with soap, they do not get into the food and nobody gets ill.

109399.q: What does the label “best before” mean?
a: Until then the manufacturer guarantees the quality
After that the product is poisonous
From then on you may eat it
That is when it was made
109399.e: The best-before date says until when an unopened product will safely keep its quality. Many foods are still fine to eat afterwards.
109399.m: Much food is still fine to eat after the best-before date.

109400.q: Which label is printed on highly perishable foods such as mince?
109400.e: Highly perishable products carry a use-by date. You should not eat them after this date, because dangerous germs could have formed.
109400.m: Do not eat a food after its use-by date.

109402.q: How do you check a yoghurt whose best-before date has passed?
a: Look at it, smell it and taste it
Freeze it and then eat it
109402.e: You can use your senses to check well whether a product is still all right. If it looks, smells and tastes normal, you can usually still eat it.
109402.m: When the best-before date has passed, your eyes, nose and tongue help.

109403.q: Which pack does the best-before date apply to?
a: To every pack in the bin
109403.e: The date applies only as long as the pack is sealed and stored correctly. Once opened, a product can go off more quickly.
109403.m: The best-before date applies to the sealed pack.

109404.q: Which food normally has no best-before date?
109404.e: Table salt practically never goes off and so needs no best-before date. Dairy products and cold meats, on the other hand, always carry a date.
109404.m: Salt does not go off and needs no expiry date.

109405.q: Which food is usually still good for some time after its best-before date?
109405.e: Dry foods such as pasta, rice or sugar often keep long past the date if stored dry. Fresh meat, fish and raw milk, on the other hand, go off quickly.
109405.m: Dry store-cupboard food often keeps longer than the printed date.

109406.e: Salmonella are rod-shaped bacteria. They can cause stomach and gut illnesses.

109407.q: Which illness do salmonella usually cause?
109407.e: Salmonella infection typically causes diarrhoea, stomach cramps, nausea and sometimes fever. It is usually passed on through contaminated food.
109407.m: Salmonella usually cause diarrhoea and tummy ache.

109408.q: In which foods are salmonella found especially often?
109408.e: Salmonella are often found in raw poultry and raw eggs. Dishes with raw eggs, such as tiramisu, should therefore be kept well chilled.
109408.m: Raw eggs and poultry need special care.

109409.q: How do you reliably make salmonella in food harmless?
109409.e: Salmonella die when the food is heated right through. When frozen, however, they survive and keep multiplying after defrosting.
109409.m: Heating food right through kills salmonella.

109410.e: The American vet Daniel Elmer Salmon ran the laboratory in which the bacteria were described in the 19th century. The genus was named after him.
109410.m: Salmonella bear the name of the vet Daniel Salmon.

109411.q: Which pets especially often carry salmonella without seeming ill?
109411.e: Many reptiles such as tortoises, lizards and snakes shed salmonella without being ill themselves. So you should wash your hands thoroughly after touching them.
109411.m: Wash your hands after touching reptiles.

109412.q: Which serious illness is caused by a particular type of salmonella?
109412.e: Typhoid is caused by Salmonella Typhi. The disease is widespread in countries with poor water supplies.
109412.m: Typhoid is caused by a type of salmonella.

109413.q: How long does it usually take from catching salmonella to the first symptoms?
a: A few hours to about 3 days
109413.e: The incubation period of salmonella infection is short, usually a few hours to a few days. That is why the cause is often a meal from the day before.
109413.m: Salmonella usually make you ill within hours to a few days.

109414.e: Prevention comes from the Latin “praevenire”, to come before. Addiction prevention aims to stop an addiction from developing at all.
109414.m: Prevention means stopping something before it starts.

109415.q: What is a typical feature of an addiction?
109415.e: Someone who is addicted can no longer decide for themselves how much they use or when they stop. Experts call this loss of control.
109415.m: With an addiction, you lose control over your use.

109416.q: What are the unpleasant symptoms called when an addict suddenly stops using their drug?
109416.e: The body has got used to the substance. When it is missing, withdrawal symptoms such as restlessness, shaking or sleep problems appear.
109416.m: Withdrawal symptoms show that the body is dependent.

109417.q: What is pressure from friends to join in with something called?
109417.e: Peer pressure arises when you want to belong. Anyone who can say “no” is better protected against risky use.
109417.m: Saying no protects against peer pressure.

109418.q: Which addiction is a behavioural addiction without a substance?
109418.e: In gambling addiction, no substance is taken. It is the behaviour itself, gambling for money, that causes the dependence.
109418.m: A behaviour such as gambling can also be addictive.

109419.q: Which phone number do children and teenagers in Switzerland call for advice when they are worried?
109419.e: On the number 147, Pro Juventute advises children and teenagers around the clock. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 144 the ambulance.
109419.m: The number 147 helps young people in Switzerland when they are worried.

109420.q: What best strengthens children and teenagers against the dangers of addiction?
a: As much screen time as possible
109420.e: Anyone who believes in themselves, can solve problems and feels supported by others is less likely to turn to drugs. Such protective factors are at the heart of addiction prevention.
109420.m: Self-confidence and good friendships protect against addiction.

109421.q: Which federal office in Switzerland is responsible for health and national prevention programmes?
109421.e: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) runs national strategies, for example on addiction and non-communicable diseases. It works with the cantons and specialist bodies to do this.
109421.m: The FOPH looks after the health of the population in Switzerland.

109422.q: Which plant does nicotine come from?
109422.e: Nicotine is found naturally in the leaves of the tobacco plant. The plant uses it to protect itself from insects.
109422.m: Nicotine comes from the tobacco plant.

109423.q: Which substance in tobacco smoke is mainly what makes people addicted?
109423.e: Nicotine acts on the reward system in the brain and quickly makes people addicted. Tar and other substances mainly harm the lungs and blood vessels.
109423.m: Nicotine is the substance that makes smokers addicted.

109424.q: How quickly does nicotine reach the brain when someone smokes?
109424.e: Through the lungs, nicotine gets into the blood very quickly and reaches the brain within seconds. This fast effect adds greatly to the addiction.
109424.m: Nicotine reaches the brain in seconds.

109425.e: The French envoy Jean Nicot brought tobacco to the French court in the 16th century. The tobacco plant Nicotiana and nicotine bear his name.
109425.m: Nicotine is named after the Frenchman Jean Nicot.

109426.q: What else was nicotine used for in the past?
109426.e: Nicotine is a strong nerve poison. That is why it used to be used against insects; today this is banned in many countries.

109427.q: What is heated and breathed in with an e-cigarette?
109427.e: An e-cigarette vaporises a liquid that often contains nicotine. Even without burning, the vapour can contain harmful substances.
109427.m: E-cigarettes vaporise a liquid that often contains nicotine.

109428.q: Which poisonous gas in tobacco smoke hinders the transport of oxygen in the blood?
109428.e: Carbon monoxide binds much more strongly to the red blood pigment than oxygen does. As a result, the blood carries less oxygen.
109428.m: Carbon monoxide from tobacco smoke robs the blood of oxygen.

109430.e: Snus is moist tobacco in small pouches that are placed under the lip. The nicotine gets into the blood through the lining of the mouth.
109430.m: Snus is placed under the lip and contains nicotine.

109431.q: Which form of media addiction has the WHO included as an illness in ICD-11?
109431.e: The World Health Organization lists gaming addiction (“gaming disorder”) in its list of diseases, ICD-11. ICD-11 has been in force since 2022.
109431.m: Gaming addiction is recognised as an illness by the WHO.

109432.q: What is a warning sign of media addiction?
109432.e: Anyone who neglects friends, hobbies and school because of their phone or games is showing a warning sign. Loss of control and irritability without the device often come too.
109432.m: If media make you neglect everything else, take care.

109433.q: What does the abbreviation FOMO stand for?
109433.e: FOMO stands for “fear of missing out”. The fear of missing something makes many people check their phone constantly.
109433.m: FOMO is the fear of missing out.

109434.q: Which sleep hormone is held back by bright screen light in the evening?
109434.e: Blue light from screens holds back the production of melatonin. You get tired later and find it harder to fall asleep.
109434.m: Screen light in the evening disturbs sleep.

109435.q: What is it called when someone ignores the person they are with and looks at their phone?
109435.e: Phubbing is made up of “phone” and “snubbing”. The other person often feels they are not being taken seriously.
109435.m: Phubbing means ignoring others because of your phone.

109436.q: Which messenger substance in the brain plays a part when likes give us a good feeling?
109436.e: Dopamine is a messenger substance of the reward system. Rewards such as likes or winning in games can release it and make you want more.
109436.m: Dopamine creates the feeling of reward in the brain.

109437.q: What is a sensible rule against too much screen time?
a: Always keep your phone within reach
Only stop when the battery is flat
109437.e: Fixed times without a phone, for example during meals or homework, help keep media use under control.
109437.m: Fixed phone times help against too much screen time.

109438.q: Which app feature tempts you to keep swiping because the content never ends?
109438.e: With infinite scrolling, new content keeps loading. There is no natural stopping point, so you easily lose track of time.
109438.m: Infinite scrolling makes time on your phone fly by.

109439.q: What helps against too much phone time at night?
a: Charging the phone outside the bedroom
Putting the phone under your pillow
109439.e: If the phone is not next to the bed, no messages disturb your sleep. That makes it easier not to look at the screen again.
109439.m: The phone sleeps best in another room.

109440.q: Where does the foundation Addiction Switzerland work?
a: Only in the canton of Zurich
109440.e: Addiction Switzerland is based in Lausanne but works for the whole of Switzerland and in several national languages.
109440.m: Addiction Switzerland works for the whole of Switzerland.

109441.q: What kind of organisation is Addiction Switzerland?
109441.e: Addiction Switzerland is a non-profit, independent foundation. It does research, provides information and campaigns for prevention.
109441.m: Addiction Switzerland is a non-profit foundation.

109442.q: What is Addiction Switzerland called in French?
109442.e: The foundation works in several national languages. In French it is known as “Addiction Suisse”; in German it is called “Sucht Schweiz”.
109442.m: Addiction Suisse is the French name of Addiction Switzerland.

109443.q: How does Addiction Switzerland find out how many young people smoke or drink alcohol?
109443.e: Addiction Switzerland regularly surveys pupils aged 11 to 15, anonymously and voluntarily. This shows how use is changing.
109443.m: Addiction Switzerland asks young people about their behaviour.

109444.q: Why does the foundation have the general name “Addiction Switzerland”?
a: It deals with all kinds of addiction
109444.e: In the past, alcohol was the main focus. Today it covers all forms of addiction, from tobacco and cannabis to gambling and online addiction.
109444.m: Addiction Switzerland deals with all forms of addiction.

109445.q: Which tasks does Addiction Switzerland carry out?
109445.e: Addiction Switzerland develops prevention projects, researches addictive behaviour and informs professionals, parents and young people. Punishment and police work are not part of it.
109445.m: Addiction Switzerland does research, informs and works to prevent addiction.

109446.q: Which topics does Addiction Switzerland deal with?
109446.e: The foundation deals with substances such as alcohol, tobacco and cannabis. Behavioural addictions such as gambling and online addiction are also included.
109446.m: Addiction Switzerland deals with substance and behavioural addictions.

109447.q: From what age are you usually allowed to buy beer and wine in Switzerland?
109447.e: In most cantons, beer and wine may be sold from the age of 16. A higher age limit applies to spirits.
109447.m: In Switzerland, beer and wine are usually available from 16.

109448.q: From what age may spirits such as schnapps be sold in Switzerland?
109448.e: Under the Alcohol Act, spirits may not be sold to anyone under 18. This also includes alcopops.
109448.m: Schnapps and alcopops are only available from 18.

109449.q: Since October 2024, from what age may tobacco products be sold throughout Switzerland?
109449.e: Under the Tobacco Products Act, sales to minors have been banned throughout Switzerland since 1 October 2024. This also applies to e-cigarettes.
109449.m: In Switzerland, tobacco and e-cigarettes are only available from 18.

109450.q: Why may alcopops only be sold from 18 in Switzerland?
109450.e: Alcopops are sweet mixed drinks containing spirits. Because they contain distilled spirits, the age limit of 18 applies.
109450.m: Alcopops contain spirits and are for over-18s only.

109451.q: What do the PEGI labels on video games stand for?
a: The country where it was made
109451.e: PEGI is a European system for age-rating games. The levels 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18 show from what age a game is suitable.
109451.m: PEGI numbers show from what age a game is suitable.
